question: to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

Third countries are increasingly instrumentalising migratory flows as a strategic tool to exert pressure against the EU, with disruptive consequences. Although the Commission identified a firm return policy as an absolute priority1, it appears that in 2025 only 28 % of those subject to expulsion orders actually left the territory of the EU2. This structural failure is inherent in the centralised approach that frames migration as a shared responsibility. Indeed, this European dogma deprives sovereign Member States of the necessary policy leeway and diplomatic tools to act effectively in their own right, lest they incur EU sanctions. The following questions thus arise: 1.
How does the Commission explain the gap between the promised 100 % commitment and the actual 28 % expulsion rate?

Does the Commission recognise national sovereignty, and is it prepared – given the failure of the European approach – to return migration policy competences to the Member States, which can regulate it more effectively, without using EU sanctions as a sword of Damocles?

Is the Commission prepared to include strict return clauses in trade agreements, which automatically lead to the freezing of preferential trade agreements in the event of noncompliance, and to provide more effective diplomatic room for manoeuvre for Member States to respond to the cries for help from the indigenous population, which is suffering under the strain of disruptive mass migration?

answer: (English version) to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE) (11 June 2026) Subject: Instrumentalisation of migration flows and political coercion of Member States Third countries are increasingly instrumentalising migratory flows as a strategic tool to exert pressure against the EU, with disruptive consequences. Although the Commission identified a firm return policy as an absolute priority (1), it appears that in 2025 only 28% of those subject to expulsion orders actually left the territory of the EU (2). This structural failure is inherent in the centralised approach that frames migration as a shared responsibility. Indeed, this European dogma deprives sovereign Member States of the necessary policy leeway and diplomatic tools to act effectively in their own right, lest they incur EU sanctions. The following questions thus arise: 1.
How does the Commission explain the gap between the promised 100% commitment and the actual 28% expulsion rate?

Does the Commission recognise national sovereignty, and is it prepared — given the failure of the European approach — to return migration policy competences to the Member States, which can regulate it more effectively, without using EU sanctions as a sword of Damocles?

Is the Commission prepared to include strict return clauses in trade agreements, which automatically lead to the freezing of preferential trade agreements in the event of non-compliance, and to provide more effective diplomatic room for manoeuvre for Member States to respond to the cries for help from the indigenous population, which is suffering under the strain of disruptive mass migration?

(16 September 2026) With swifter, simpler and more effective procedures across the EU, when in force, the Return Regulation (1) will give Member States better tools to address these shortcomings in full respect of fundamental rights. In parallel, the Commission, together with Member States, is continuing to work with third countries to increase cooperation on readmission. Pursuant to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the immigration policy is a shared competence between the Member States and the EU. The European Parliament and the Council have agreed to reform the return policy and to legislate with a regulation. The regulation aims at increasing the efficiency of returns and will complement the Pact on Migration and Asylum (2) that is applicable since 12 June 2026. The EU is developing a comprehensive toolkit of leverages to incentivise better cooperation on readmission of partner countries. Under visa policy (3), the mechanism under Article 25a of the Visa Code (4) has proven its effectiveness to enhance third countries’ cooperation on readmission. The new Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) (5), effective from 2027, introduces the possibility of suspending trade benefits for countries that fail to cooperate on readmission.

To ensure synergies of tools, the Commission proposal for the Global Europe Regulation (6) for 2028-2034 includes the possibility to suspend payments or the implementation of a programme, in case the Commission, in consultation with the European External Action Service, identify serious shortcomings in a partner country related in particular to the obligation to readmit its own nationals.
